conceptTag: The 1970s gas lines and price controls
readerTitle: Why Americans waited hours for gas in the 1970s
caseNote: 실제 사건 (1973~74년 석유 금수 조치와 미국 휘발유 가격 통제, 1979년 2차 석유 파동, 1981년 가격 통제 해제) + 가상 적용 (브런치 식당, 냉방 수리 업체, 소프트웨어 대기 명단)
insight: 가격을 시장 수준보다 낮게 묶어도 비용은 사라지지 않는다. 고객은 돈 대신 시간과 수고로 값을 치르고, 그 값은 공급을 늘리는 데 쓰이지 않고 그냥 사라진다.
misconception: 가격을 낮게 묶으면 고객이 보호받는다. 줄이 길어지는 건 공급이 부족해서이지 가격 때문이 아니다.

sources.text: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian, "Oil Embargo, 1973–1974" (금수 조치 시기, 유가 약 4배 상승)
Federal Reserve History, "Oil Shock of 1973–74" (가격 통제, 주유소 대기 줄, 홀짝제)
Federal Reserve History, "Oil Shock of 1978–79" (1979년 대기 줄 재발)
Emergency Petroleum Allocation Act of 1973 (석유 가격 통제와 배분 규칙)
Executive Order 12287, "Decontrol of Crude Oil and Refined Petroleum Products" (1981년 1월)
Nixon 대통령의 1973년 11월 에너지 연설 (주유소 일요일 휴업 요청)

factChecks.note: 금수 조치 기간(1973년 10월~1974년 3월)과 유가가 약 4배 올랐다는 점을 국무부 역사실 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 "roughly four times"로만 적었습니다.
미국의 가격 통제가 1971년 8월 닉슨의 임금·가격 동결에서 시작해 석유 부문에 남았다는 점을 확인하세요. 카드에는 "federal price controls, in place since 1971"로 적었습니다.
홀짝제(번호판 끝자리), 일요일 휴업 요청, 1회 구매량 제한은 일부 주와 주유소에서 시행되었습니다. 전국 공통 규칙이 아니었다는 점을 카드 문구("some states", "many stations")에 반영했습니다. 대기 시간은 자료마다 달라 구체적인 숫자를 쓰지 않았습니다.
배분 규칙이 과거 사용량을 기준으로 해서 지역 간 불균형이 생겼다는 설명은 경제사 문헌에 자주 나옵니다. 출처를 하나 더 확보하고 문구를 확인하세요.
운전자들이 탱크를 자주 채워 줄이 더 길어졌다는 설명(topping off)은 당시 보도와 경제사 문헌에 자주 나옵니다. 규모는 불확실해서 정성적으로만 적었습니다.
1981년 1월 레이건 행정명령 12287로 남은 통제가 해제된 점을 확인하세요. 1990년 걸프전 유가 급등 때 전국적인 대기 줄이 재발하지 않았다는 문구도 확인이 필요합니다. 지역 단위 품귀(허리케인, 2021년 송유관 사고 등)는 있었기 때문에 "long national lines"로 범위를 좁혀 적었습니다.
가격 통제가 대기 줄의 주된 원인이었다는 점은 경제학자들 사이에서 널리 받아들여지는 해석입니다. 다만 공급 충격, 배분 규칙, 사재기 심리도 함께 작용했다는 점을 Watch out 카드와 본문에 반영했습니다.

cards.title: Why Americans waited hours for gas in the 1970s
body: In the winter of 1973–74, cars lined up around the block at American gas stations. Some drivers waited hours. Some reached the pump just as it ran dry.
The oil supply had been cut. But the lines grew long for another reason: the price of gasoline wasn't allowed to rise.

image.label: A long line of 1970s cars waiting at a gas station
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1970년대 둥근 자동차들이 주유소 앞에 길게 줄 서 있고, 주유기에 "Sorry, no gas" 표지판. 하늘은 겨울 오후 빛. 실제 정유사 로고나 브랜드 색은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run a gas station in 1973.
body: Your supplier just cut your monthly delivery. Federal rules cap the price you can charge. By 9 a.m., the line reaches the next street.
You can't raise the price. What do you do?

options.text: Sell to everyone, first come, first served, until the tanks are empty
options.feedback: Simple and feels fair. But the gas goes to whoever can wait longest, and you may be empty by noon.

options.text: Limit each car to 10 gallons and shorten your hours
options.feedback: More drivers get some gas. But many come back the next day to top up, so the line never really shrinks.

options.text: Save most of the gas for your regular customers
options.feedback: You protect relationships that will outlast the crisis. Strangers, including people with urgent trips, get nothing.

choice.afterReveal: Each option decides who gets the gas. None of them adds a single gallon. With the price fixed, something other than price has to do the sorting.

cards.title: The oil price soared. The pump price couldn't follow.
body: In October 1973, Arab oil producers stopped selling oil to the United States. Over the next months, world oil prices rose to **roughly four times** their earlier level.
In the U.S., federal price controls, in place since 1971, held down what stations could charge. So gasoline stayed cheap on paper and ran short in practice.
Many stations limited purchases or closed on Sundays. Some states let drivers buy only on odd or even days, matched to their license plate.

cards.title: A price ceiling turns a shortage into a line.
body: A **price ceiling** is a legal maximum price. When it sits below the price where supply and demand would meet, people want to buy more than sellers can offer.
Something still has to decide who gets the scarce goods. If money can't do it, time does. Drivers paid the capped price at the pump, plus hours of their day in line.

image.label: Supply and demand chart with a price cap below the meeting point
image.brief: 간단한 수요·공급 그래프. 두 곡선이 만나는 점보다 아래에 빨간 가로선 "Price cap". 가로선 위에서 수요와 공급 사이의 틈을 "Shortage"로 표시하고, 그 틈에 작은 자동차 줄 아이콘을 넣음.

cards.title: Waiting is a price nobody collects.
body: A money price and a time price both ration. But they work very differently.
list: **A higher money price** goes to the seller, which pays for more supply and tells suppliers where to send it
**A time price** goes to no one; the hours in line are simply lost
**Fear of running out** made drivers fill up more often, so lines grew longer
**Allocation rules** based partly on past use sent fuel to the wrong places as needs shifted
cards.callout: A money price pulls in more supply. A line just burns time.

cards.title: The lines came back, then went away for good.
body: After the 1979 Iranian Revolution disrupted oil supply, the lines returned, especially in California. Price controls were still in place.
In January 1981, President Reagan ended the remaining federal controls on oil prices. Prices rose at first and fell through much of the 1980s.
When oil prices spiked again in 1990, prices at the pump jumped quickly. The long national lines did not return.

cards.title: The same thing happens at a brunch spot.
body: A popular café keeps its brunch at $14, well below what weekend crowds would pay. By 10 a.m. the wait is 90 minutes.
Customers still pay more than $14. They pay in waiting. Regulars who can't spare the time quietly stop coming, and the café earns nothing extra from the crowd outside.
cards.softwareNote: A launch with limited seats priced far below their value works the same way. Users pay with waitlists and referral hoops, and sometimes accounts get resold. The demand is real, but none of that extra value funds more capacity.

cards.title: Holding a price can be the right call.
body: Higher prices hurt people who can't afford them, and customers often see sudden spikes in a crisis as unfair. Many places also have rules against raising prices sharply in emergencies.
The 1970s lines also had other causes: a real supply shock, clumsy allocation rules and panic buying.
So the lesson isn't "always raise the price." It's this: if you keep a price low, decide on purpose how you'll ration. Otherwise the line decides for you.

cards.title: Now it's a heat wave.
body: You run an air-conditioning repair company. A heat wave hits. Your crews can handle 20 calls a day. Sixty people are calling.
Your normal rate is fair and customers trust it. What do you do?

options.text: Keep normal rates and book everyone in the order they call
options.feedback: Your prices stay friendly, but an elderly client with no cooling may wait behind a routine tune-up. Customers pay in days of waiting.

options.text: Keep normal rates for scheduled work, add a clear same-day emergency fee, and put the most urgent calls first
options.feedback: Price and priority both help ration. Urgent jobs get done first, the fee pays for overtime crews, and regular customers keep the price they trust.

options.text: Double all your prices until the heat wave ends
options.feedback: The line shrinks and revenue rises, but customers may remember you as the company that cashed in on a crisis.

cards.title: If price can't ration, something else will.
body: Holding a price below demand doesn't remove the cost. Customers pay it in time, hassle or missed service, and none of it pays for more supply.
**Try it today:** find where your customers wait, such as a booking calendar, a queue or a backorder list. Ask what is really doing the rationing there.
